report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Executive summary

What happened

On 07/07/2026, MV Tarrakin Star, a 24.4 m aluminium catamaran passenger ferry certificated for 96 passengers, grounded on Boolarong Bank in the Merrandi Channel, Kanooka Heads, while inbound on service TF18. Times in this report are local time (UTC+10). Contact was at 18:12:04 at 6.8 kt over the ground, in darkness on a falling tide. There were 38 passengers, a master, a deckhand and a kiosk attendant on board.

There were no serious injuries. One passenger reported a grazed shin and two were treated at the wharf for distress. All 38 passengers were ashore by 19:26. The vessel was substantially damaged, with a 180 mm split in the starboard hull plating and flooding of the No. 2 void, and was withdrawn from service after refloating at 00:20. The Merrandi Channel was closed to commercial traffic for 19 hours. The master stopped both engines 27 seconds after contact and made no attempt to refloat, which very likely reduced risk because the hull was holed.

What the investigation found

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the probable cause statement in the application's wording]

The chart plotter display froze at 18:07:06. The master continued at eight knots without a position fix, and the heading eased from 195 to 200 degrees without a decision to turn. The No. 4 beacon, the only remaining reference, was screened by mangroves from 0.84 to 0.34 nm. The vessel crossed the western edge of the dredged channel at about 18:09:00. The shallow alarm, set at 0.9 m, gave 16 seconds' warning against a 92 m crash stop distance.

The plotter freeze very likely contributed because no position fix was available afterwards, and continuing at eight knots very likely contributed because a stop in the 114 seconds before the edge would have left the vessel in the channel. The screened beacon likely contributed to the heading change going unnoticed, although the heading change began before the search and the light was clear of the islet for at least the last 37 seconds. The alarm setting very likely contributed because 16 seconds was less than the stopping distance allowed.

The last service was moved into darkness without reopening the daylight-only route risk assessment, which likely contributed to the absence of a night passage plan. That absence very likely contributed to the transit continuing, because nothing asked the master to stop. The defect procedure did not require a fault that had cleared itself to be recorded, which likely contributed to the freeze because the firmware fix was never applied. The clearing of the beacon's sightline was deferred unfunded at three works rounds, which very likely contributed to the screening.

Two matters could not be settled. Whether unshielded boat ramp floodlights behind the beacon delayed its sighting is about as likely as not and still being examined. Whether the master was fatigued is also about as likely as not, and neither is carried into the findings.

What can be done

A passage plan should name what to do if the primary means of position fixing is lost, and a timetable change into darkness should reopen the risk assessment. Defect reporting should capture faults that clear themselves. Authorities should not make work needed to keep an aid visible depend on its distance from the structure.

The canopy was trimmed to 2 m on 24/07/2026 under WO-176. Local notice LNM-2026-14 was issued on 22/07/2026, and Tarrakin Ferries reissued its passage plan appendix as issue 3. Two recommendations are open, with responses due 30/09/2026: to replace the 50 m vegetation scope with a sightline test, and that Tarrakin Ferries write a night passage plan with a hold point before any further darkness transit. Other safety issues, including the lifejacket locker arrangement still being examined, have no recorded action.

Factual information

This section sets out the facts of the occurrence involving MV Tarrakin Star on 07/07/2026, drawn from the recorded data, documents, surveys and accounts gathered.

History of the occurrence

Before the voyage

The outgoing master finished the morning shift and handed over to the master at the town wharf at about 13:05. The outgoing master told the master that the chart plotter had frozen twice that morning and had recovered itself both times. The master replied that it had done the same the month before. Neither entered the fault in the wheelhouse defect book, and no entry of any kind was made for 07/07/2026 before the occurrence.

The voyage

MV Tarrakin Star, a 24.4 m aluminium catamaran passenger ferry certificated for 96 passengers, departed Muntari Island jetty at 17:35:02 on service TF18 and reported its departure to Port Control on VHF channel 12 with 38 passengers. Port Control replied that the channel was clear. A master, a deckhand and a kiosk attendant were also on board. Sunset had been at 17:02 and civil twilight ended at 17:29. TF18 was the last service of the day and the thirty-first darkness transit of the winter timetable since 01/06/2026.

The vessel entered the Merrandi Channel from the north at 18:03:58 at 8.4 kt on a course of 195 degrees, 2 m east of the charted centreline. The bridge audio records the deckhand asking at 18:04:10 whether to stay on the bridge. The master replied at 18:04:14 that the deckhand should go and collect the fares. No lookout remained on the bridge from that time.

At 18:05:30 the vessel was abeam the No. 2 beacon, 1 m west of the centreline, with speed and course unchanged. The plotter's event log records the display process not responding at 18:07:06, when the vessel was 3 m west of the centreline. The bridge audio records "Oh, come on" at 18:07:11, sound consistent with repeated screen taps at 18:07:26, and "(unintelligible) frozen again" at 18:07:44.

At 18:08:31 the master said "Right. Where's four". The vessel was then 12 m west of the centreline and 0.47 nm north of the No. 4 beacon. By 18:09:00 the vessel was 20 m west of the centreline, at the western edge of the dredged channel, 0.40 nm north of the beacon. Sound consistent with a window or door being slid open was recorded at 18:09:40.

At 18:10:02 the master said "There's four. Bring her back". The vessel was then 39 m west of the centreline and 0.25 nm north of the beacon, outside the dredged channel. At 18:11:00 it was 58 m west and over Boolarong Bank. The echo sounder shallow alarm began at 18:11:48 with the vessel 70 m west. At 18:11:52 both throttles were moved to astern together. At 18:12:04 the vessel made contact with Boolarong Bank at 6.8 kt over the ground. It came to rest within 11 m, heeled 4 degrees to starboard, on a falling tide. The surveyed position was 74 m west of the charted centreline, 54 m outside the dredged channel and 34 m west of the No. 4 beacon. The bridge audio records sustained grinding and vibration for approximately 9 seconds.

The AIS and recorder readout is the investigator's description of what was observed. In summary, speed over the ground was 8.4 kt at the freeze and 8.1 kt at 18:08:00, and fell to 7.1 kt by 18:11:48 with no throttle movement recorded until 18:11:52. Course over ground increased from 195 to 200 degrees between 18:07:06 and 18:10:02, then eased to 197 degrees by contact.

The response

Both engines were stopped at 18:12:31 and were not restarted. The master addressed passengers by public address at 18:12:40. At 18:13:04 the master broadcast a pan pan on VHF channel 16, stating "I am not attempting to refloat", and Port Control acknowledged and called the workboat at 18:13:29. The master addressed passengers again at 18:14:52 and directed that lifejackets be issued.

The deckhand reported water in the No. 2 void at 18:16:20, about two or three inches on the sounding rod, and the master directed that it be sounded every ten minutes. At 18:17:05 the master reported to Port Control approximately 75 mm of ingress into the No. 2 starboard void. At 18:22:40 the deckhand reported that everyone was in a jacket and that two people in the forward saloon had required the deckhand to go round the servery, as the locker was behind the counter. The workboat came alongside at 18:41 and the last passenger was ashore at 19:26:08. The vessel refloated on the rising tide at 00:20 on 08/07/2026 and was towed to the town wharf. The Merrandi Channel was closed to commercial traffic for 19 hours.

Injuries to persons

There were no serious injuries. One passenger reported a grazed shin and two were treated at the wharf for distress.

Damage

The post-grounding survey, the investigator's description of what was observed, found the starboard hull bottom plating set up over 4.1 m between frames 6 and 11, with a 180 mm split in way of the No. 2 void. Ingress into that void was about 75 mm at 18:16 and approximately 260 mm when the vessel refloated. All three blades of the starboard propeller were bent aft, the shaft was bent 1.4 mm, the starboard rudder stock was distorted 3 degrees and the starboard skeg was torn away. No damage was found to the port hull, propulsion or steering.

The bed at the contact point was 0.50 m below chart datum, rising to 0.15 m below datum 30 m further west, so the bed 30 m further west was 0.35 m higher. Furrows consistent with the starboard hull and skeg run 11 m from the point of first contact on a heading of 197 degrees.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the vessel's registration, flag, owner and class details]. The operator is Tarrakin Ferries.

Personnel information

The master held a master's certificate for sheltered-waters passenger vessels, held since 2012. The master had 14 years as master, 11 of them with Tarrakin Ferries and on this route, and had made approximately 4,100 transits of the Merrandi Channel. The last route check, on 14/02/2026, was satisfactory. The master had no prior occurrence history and had made 26 of the 30 darkness transits of the channel before the occurrence.

The 07/07/2026 duty was the master's ninth consecutive day of a twelve-day tour, on a split duty of 05:40 to 08:40 on another of the operator's vessels and 13:00 to 19:20 on MV Tarrakin Star. That gave 9 hours 20 minutes of duty across a spread of 13 hours 40 minutes, against the operator's limits of 10 hours of duty and 14 hours of spread. The master recorded 6 hours 15 minutes of sleep the night before in the fatigue diary that the operator asks masters to keep but does not collect.

The outgoing master had 9 years as master, 4 of them on this route, and about 1,400 transits of the channel. The outgoing master was on day six of a twelve-day tour and had made the other 4 of the 30 darkness transits.

The deckhand had been with the operator 7 months, held a basic marine safety certificate and a coxswain's certificate, and was in the first winter season on the route.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the kiosk attendant's role details, qualifications or account].

Meteorological information

The Kanooka Heads weather station recorded wind from 305 to 310 degrees at 7 to 9 kt between 17:30 and 18:30, visibility over 10 km and no rainfall since 09:00. The port workboat reported a slight sea in the channel at 18:45, with wind ripple only and no swell penetrating the entrance. Moonrise was at 06:12, a waning crescent 2% illuminated. The transit was made 35 minutes after the end of civil twilight, in darkness.

The predicted tide height at 18:12 was 0.94 m, and the Port Authority gauge at Kanooka Heads recorded 0.91 m. Low water was predicted at 21:34.

Recorded data

The plotter is a 12-inch multifunction display fed by a separate GPS antenna unit, running chart software revision 4.11 on firmware issued 03/2024. Its internal event log, as described by the investigator, records a watchdog reset with cause code 0x51 (display process not responding) at 10:42 and 11:17 on 07/07/2026, from which the unit recovered itself. At 18:07:06 the log records the display process not responding with no reset. The unit was bench tested by an approved electronics contractor for 46 hours on 21/07/2026 using the same antenna and cabling. The fault did not recur and no defect was found. The contractor's report noted that cause code 0x51 is known to the manufacturer and is addressed by firmware issued in 11/2024, which had not been applied to this unit.

The engine monitoring recorder, as described by the investigator, shows both engines at 1,780 and 1,784 rpm, within 12 rpm of each other, from 18:03 to 18:11:52, with no alarm and no throttle movement. Steering gear hydraulic pressure was 96 to 99 bar against a normal band of 90 to 105 bar. Rudder angle followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees throughout. The rate of turn peaked at 6 degrees per minute at 18:07:40 and returned to zero by 18:08:50. On 12/07/2026 the steering gear's rams, tiller arms, hydraulic system and autopilot were removed and function tested, and all were serviceable.

The echo sounder's shallow alarm was set at 0.9 m under the keel, the value written into the setup at commissioning in 2019, and was not changed. It sounded once on the voyage, at 18:11:48, 16 seconds before contact. At 7.1 kt the vessel covered 58 m in that time. The vessel's trials figure for a crash stop from 8 kt is 92 m. The bank gradient across the section was about 1 in 70.

Aids to navigation and the channel

The Merrandi Channel is 40 m wide, dredged to 3.2 m, and is not a declared shipping channel. It is a dredged recreational and commercial access channel on a waterway managed by Kanooka Shire Council through the Kanooka Heads Port Authority.

The No. 4 beacon (Fl G 2.5s) was converted from a mains supply to a solar lantern in 11/2025. The replacement lantern is rated at a nominal 3 nautical miles, against 6 for the lantern it replaced. A notification was lodged with the hydrographic service on 04/02/2026 and the chart correction was still pending on 07/07/2026. No local notice to mariners was issued. The beacon's luminous range, measured from the port workboat on 18/07/2026, was 2.6 nm. The lantern is 4.2 m above chart datum.

The range and visibility check of 18/07/2026, made on the inbound track at the same time of night, found that the beacon is not visible from the channel between 0.84 nm and 0.34 nm north of it. The sightline over that stretch passes through the mangrove canopy on Merrandi Islet, about 240 m north of the beacon in the shoal strip between the dredged western edge and the bank. The canopy measured 5.8 m, against 2.1 m in the 2019 aerial survey. The check was made on the inbound track, and a vessel west of that track sees the light open earlier. The vessel passed about 24 m west of the islet at about 18:11.

The Port Authority's register records work order WO-118, raised 09/2023, for mangrove regrowth screening the No. 4 beacon from the northern approach between about half a mile and a quarter mile. It recommended trimming to 2 m on a three-yearly cycle at an estimated $18,500. It was deferred at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 works rounds, each entry reading "defer, unfunded, refer next round". Work order WO-176, raised 03/2026, records the same sightline as "now fully closed on the northern approach". The Authority's file note records that the islet is 240 m from the beacon and so falls outside the 50 m scope of schedule 2.4, and that the work therefore competed in the general waterways vote with boat ramps and pontoons. The beacon was recorded as "observed, operating" on the monthly check in every month from 01/2024 to 07/2026. The check is made from the town wharf, 2.1 nm south of the beacon, from which the islet is not in the line of sight. No defect has ever been recorded against the beacon, no notice about it has ever been issued to a waterway user, and the Authority holds no record of any operator asking about the channel's aids. The register had never been provided to Tarrakin Ferries.

Section 4 of the Waterways Aids to Navigation Code WAN-2 provides:

  • "4.1 The authority responsible for an aid to navigation must maintain it so that it performs the function for which it was established." (WAN-2)
  • "4.2 Where an aid to navigation is established on a declared shipping channel, the responsible authority must record its availability, must achieve an availability of not less than 99.0 per cent measured annually, and must notify a change to the aid's character, position or range by notice to mariners before the change takes effect." (WAN-2)
  • "4.3 Where an aid to navigation is established on a waterway that is not a declared shipping channel, section 4.2 does not apply. The responsible authority must be able to demonstrate that the aid is inspected at intervals it has determined and recorded." (WAN-2)

The services agreement between the Council and the Authority provides in schedule 2:

  • "S2.1 The Authority will inspect each lit aid by daylight once per quarter and will confirm each lit aid's operation by observation from the town wharf once per month." (services agreement)
  • "S2.4 Vegetation management within 50 m of an aid is a works item and is funded from the general waterways maintenance vote. Vegetation beyond 50 m is not within the scope of this agreement." (services agreement)
  • "S2.7 Defects found are recorded in the aids to navigation register and actioned in accordance with the Authority's maintenance priority scale. There is no requirement in this agreement to notify waterway users of a defect, a deferral or a change to an aid." (services agreement)

The foreshore redevelopment at Kanooka Heads was commissioned on 22/05/2026, ten days before the winter timetable began. The foreshore lighting survey of 18/07/2026, as described by the investigator, found 14 unshielded LED floodlights on 12 m columns lighting the new boat ramp and car park, 300 m east of the town wharf. Each presents about 4,800 candela toward the channel and none is shielded to seaward. From 0.5 nm north of the No. 4 beacon the array lies behind the beacon within 4 degrees of the same bearing and within 1.5 degrees of the same elevation. The array is continuously lit while the beacon flashes green for 0.4 seconds every 2.5 seconds. The Port Authority's aids to navigation officer was not consulted and no assessment of the lighting against the channel's aids was carried out or required. Whether these floodlights affected the sighting of the beacon is still being examined.

Organisational information

Tarrakin Ferries Operations Manual OPS-3 revision 6 (02/2023) provides:

  • "3.2 A written passage plan is held for each scheduled route. The master will conduct the passage in accordance with the plan and will record any departure from it in the deck log." (OPS-3)
  • "3.4 The Merrandi Channel transit will be made on the charted centreline, monitored on the chart plotter, with the No. 2 and No. 4 beacons identified visually before the vessel passes the No. 1 beacon." (OPS-3)
  • "3.6 In reduced visibility the master will reduce to a speed at which the vessel can be stopped within the distance in which the channel can be seen, and will consider anchoring or returning to open water." (OPS-3)

Appendix A, the Merrandi Channel passage plan, issue 2 (02/2023) and current, gives a transit speed of 8 knots and a course of 195 degrees true inbound. It names the chart plotter as the primary means of position fixing and the visual transit of the No. 4 beacon and the town wharf leading lights as the secondary means. It records the No. 4 beacon at 6 M and states that it is "written for the daylight transit" and that "Night transits are not scheduled on this route." The plan names no hold point or abort criterion and gives no guidance on what to do if the plotter is lost during the transit. The leading lights bear 195 degrees but lie about 1.9 nm beyond the No. 6 beacon and do not resolve as two lights until the vessel is inside the channel's southern third.

Operations Manual OPS-9 revision 4 (08/2024) provides:

  • "9.1 A defect which renders the vessel unseaworthy or which affects a statutory item of equipment shall be reported to the Operations Manager immediately and entered in the vessel defect book." (OPS-9)
  • "9.2 All other defects shall be entered in the vessel defect book at the end of the shift in which they are found, and will be reviewed by the Operations Manager weekly." (OPS-9)
  • "9.3 At a change of master the outgoing master will brief the relieving master on the state of the vessel, any defect, and anything else affecting the conduct of the service." (OPS-9)

The chart plotter is not a statutory item on a sheltered-waters passenger vessel on this route, although it is the primary means of position fixing named in the passage plan. The defect book carried eleven entries in the 90 days before the occurrence, none concerning the plotter, the GPS antenna, the echo sounder, the steering gear, the engines or the propulsion controls. The maintenance system held no work order, fault report or correspondence relating to the plotter in 2026. The operator held no subscription to the manufacturer's bulletins.

Route Risk Assessment RRA-07 issue 2 (03/2023) is the current assessment for the channel and no issue 3 exists. It carries the operating restriction "daylight transits only" and states that a night transit requires the General Manager Operations' approval and a specific passage plan. Change record CHG-2026-014, approved by the Operations Manager on 22/04/2026, moved TF18 from 16:15 to 17:35 for the winter timetable from 01/06/2026. It assessed the change as "timetable change only", recorded "No new hazard identified" and answered "No" to route risk assessment review required. RRA-07 was not reopened, no night passage plan was written, and the General Manager Operations' approval was neither sought nor given. TF18 ran 31 times in darkness between 01/06/2026 and the occurrence.

Five masters work the route on a 12 days on, 2 days off cycle. In the winter timetable TF18 closes the afternoon half of a split duty, 05:40 to 08:40 and 13:00 to 19:20, worked by the master on that line on every day of the tour. No relief master is rostered, and a master who reports unfit is covered by extending another master's tour.

The company reporting system has a "navigation hazard" category. It had not been used on this route in three years, and no master interviewed knew it existed.

Interviews and reports

The master

In interview the master described the changeover at about 13:05, when the outgoing master said the plotter had frozen twice and recovered. The master said: "Neither of us wrote it down." Of the entry in the defect book the master said: "It would have taken eleven seconds. But it's not a defect in your head, is it. It's a thing that happened and stopped happening." The master described the practice as general: "The book is for things that are broken when you hand over. If it's broken you write it, if it came good you say it."

Of the freeze the master said: "The picture stays there, that's the thing, it looks fine. The boat just stops moving on it." Asked whether stopping was considered, the master answered: "No. And that's the honest answer and it's not a good one. I didn't think about it. I went straight to the visual transit because in my head the visual transit is the backup." The master added: "We haven't got a night plan for that channel."

Of the search for the beacon the master said: "You're looking into a wall of light." The master described the beacon's flash as "a nothing" in front of the town and the new floodlights, and said of the vessel's heading: "I eased her to starboard while I was fiddling with the plotter and then looking for four. Five degrees. I never made that decision." On seeing the beacon dead ahead, the master brought the vessel back to port, believing it to be "just outside the edge, a boat width maybe", and said: "I was nearly forty metres out." The master said that stopping "on the edge of a bank I couldn't see, felt worse than easing her back in."

The master said the timetable change brought "A new roster sheet. That's it. No brief, no plan, no conversation." Of the earlier darkness transits the master said: "It just hadn't bitten anybody yet." Of the master's own condition the master said: "I was tired. I'd be lying if I said otherwise," and added: "I wasn't fighting to stay awake and I wasn't slow."

Of the decision not to refloat the master said: "Falling tide, unknown bottom, thirty eight people aboard." The master had told no one about the beacon's decline over two years beyond other masters and the workboat crew, and said: "There's no form for the beacon looks dim." Asked what the investigation should examine, the master said: "The beacon and the night plan. In that order."

The outgoing master

The outgoing master's account is taken from the investigator's write-up and is summarised here. The outgoing master worked the morning shift from 05:40 to 13:05 and described two plotter freezes, one on the 10:20 out of the town wharf and one on the 11:05 return, both in open water outside the channel, each clearing by itself after a minute or two. The outgoing master told the master of both at the handover and did not enter them in the defect book, not having thought of them as defects because they had cleared. The outgoing master believed the plotter had frozen on this vessel three or four times in the past year, to the outgoing master and to others, without any being written up.

Asked what would have been done had it frozen inside the channel, the outgoing master said the way would have been taken off the vessel until the display came back or the position was confirmed by the marks, and knew of no rule requiring that. The outgoing master described the No. 4 beacon as having declined over two years, and as difficult to see from up the channel since the car park lighting was installed. The outgoing master had mentioned it to the workboat crew but had never reported it, there being no route to do so. The outgoing master said that nothing but a new roster accompanied the winter timetable change.

Safety reports

The master's safety report, submitted under a just-culture scheme, is consistent with the master's interview on the changeover, the freeze, the continuation of the transit at eight knots, the search for the beacon, the heading change, the decision not to refloat and the absence of a night plan.

The deckhand's safety report raises the forward saloon lifejacket locker. The deckhand reported having to ask people at the servery counter to move and then pass round the end of the counter through a narrow gap to hand jackets out. The deckhand reported that the muster placard directs passengers to a locker that cannot be seen from the seats, and believed the arrangement to be the same on the operator's other vessels.

Forward saloon lifejacket stowage

The stowage survey of 16/07/2026, as described by the investigator, recorded that the vessel carries 120 adult and 20 child lifejackets in four lockers. The forward saloon locker holds 40 adult jackets and is mounted in the bulkhead behind the kiosk servery counter. The arrangement approved at build in 2011 had an open bench in that position with the locker face clear. The counter was fitted in a 2019 interior refit carried out under a minor modification notice that did not trigger a re-survey of the safety equipment arrangement. The locker face cannot be reached from 22 of the 34 forward saloon seats without passing behind the counter through a 0.6 m gap at its inboard end. The muster placard directs passengers to "the locker forward on the port side", which is not visible from the seats. The same counter is fitted to the operator's two other 24 m vessels. The significance of the arrangement is still being examined.

Matters not established

[NOT ESTABLISHED: a formal interview with the Operations Manager]. The only source is a verbal account not taken as a formal interview.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the regulator's and operator's answers on whether the counter arrangement is fleet-wide beyond the operator's statement].

Analysis

This analysis follows the sequence from the decision to run the service in darkness, through the loss of the plotter and the departure from the channel, to the grounding. It then deals with two matters that could not be settled, the factors that increased risk without contributing, and the matters considered and not found to contribute.

General

The master held a master's certificate for sheltered-waters passenger vessels, had about 4,100 transits of the Merrandi Channel, and had passed a route check on 14/02/2026. The vessel completed its annual survey on 11/03/2026 with no outstanding conditions. The duty on 07/07/2026 was inside the operator's limits of 10 hours of duty and 14 hours of spread.

Weather and sea played no part. The wind was 8 kt from 305 degrees, visibility was more than 10 km, and the sea in the channel was slight. There was no other traffic.

Steering and propulsion were very unlikely to have failed before the vessel left the centreline. The engines held 1,780 and 1,784 rpm within 12 rpm of each other from 18:03 to 18:11:52 with no alarm. Steering hydraulic pressure held at 96 to 99 bar against a normal band of 90 to 105 bar, and rudder angle followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees. The whole steering system was removed and tested on 12/07/2026 and every component was serviceable with no sign of a pre-existing defect. The starboard shaft, propeller and rudder damage dated from the contact.

Tide set down below prediction was very unlikely. The gauge read 0.91 m at 18:12 against 0.94 m predicted, and the largest departure from prediction in the preceding twelve hours was 0.07 m. With the bed at the contact point 0.50 m below chart datum there was 1.41 m of water over it. The vessel would have touched at the predicted tide as well, because it was 54 m outside a channel dredged to 3.2 m.

Why the transit was made in darkness without a night plan

Route Risk Assessment RRA-07 issue 2 carried the operating restriction "daylight transits only" and stated that "A night transit of the Merrandi Channel requires the General Manager Operations' approval and a specific passage plan." Change record CHG-2026-014 moved service TF18 from 16:15 to 17:35 from 01/06/2026. It assessed the change as "timetable change only", recorded "No new hazard identified" and answered "No" to route risk assessment review. The Operations Manager approved it on 22/04/2026, one level below the approver the restriction names. The change record did not refer to the restriction, RRA-07 was not reopened, and no night passage plan was written. The service then ran 31 times in darkness, the occurrence transit being the thirty-first.

A review of RRA-07 against a night operation would have reached the unlit reach between the No. 2 and No. 4 beacons, which the assessment already named as a hazard. Because the restriction named the plan, such a review could not have closed without one. The process used asked whether the change was new rather than whether the assessment still held. A reopened assessment might nonetheless have produced a night plan with no more in it than the daylight plan, and the vessel would then have met the frozen plotter in the same way. [NOT ESTABLISHED: why the change was assessed as a timetable change only, as no formal account from the Operations Manager is held]. On balance of this evidence, it is likely that moving the service into darkness without reopening the assessment contributed to the absence of a night plan.

The absence mattered because the operator's own plan was its defence against the loss of the plotter. OPS-3 3.4 required the transit to be made on the charted centreline, monitored on the chart plotter. Appendix A, issue 2, named the plotter as the primary means of fixing and the visual transit of the No. 4 beacon with the town wharf leading lights as the secondary. It closed with the note that the plan was written for the daylight transit and that night transits were not scheduled. It named no abort or hold point and gave no guidance on loss of the plotter. OPS-3 3.6 required a reduction of speed and consideration of anchoring, but only in reduced visibility, and visibility on the night was more than 10 km. The leading lights bear 195 degrees but lie about 1.9 nm beyond the No. 6 beacon and do not resolve as two lights until the vessel is inside the channel's southern third, so where the plotter was lost the beacon was the whole of the secondary means.

Both masters interviewed said independently that stopping was the right answer and that no document asks for it. The outgoing master said the way would have been taken off the vessel and the vessel left there, because there was no traffic and nothing to hit if stopped. The master had 114 seconds between the freeze and crossing the channel edge, and a named hold point would have applied throughout. A master who did not think of stopping unprompted might not have applied a written rule under the same pressure. It is very likely that the lack of a night passage plan with a hold point for loss of the primary fix contributed to the transit continuing at eight knots.

Why the plotter froze and why the fault never travelled

The plotter's event log recorded the display process not responding at 18:07:06 with no reset. The bridge audio matched it, with "Oh, come on" at 18:07:11, repeated screen taps at 18:07:26 and "frozen again" at 18:07:44. The master's account was that the picture stayed on the screen with the vessel symbol stationary and no response to touch. The contractor's 46 hour bench test on 21/07/2026 did not reproduce the fault and found no defect. The contractor did identify cause code 0x51, logged at 10:42 and 11:17 that morning, as known to the manufacturer and addressed by firmware issued in 11/2024 that this unit had never had applied. The bench test limits what can be said about the physical cause, but the three sources agree that the display froze during the transit. The freeze was a condition the transit was then made without, and it is extremely likely that it contributed to the vessel continuing without a position fix, since no fix of any kind was available between the freeze and the search for the beacon 85 seconds later.

The fault had never reached anyone able to act on it. OPS-9 9.1 required immediate reporting only of a defect that rendered the vessel unseaworthy or affected a statutory item, and the plotter was not a statutory item on this route although it was the primary means of fixing. OPS-9 9.2 required other defects to be entered at the end of the shift in which they were found, which for a fault that had come and gone gave no trigger. OPS-9 9.3 required a verbal brief at change of master and nothing written. Both masters read the procedure the same way, in the master's words that the book is for things broken at handover. The book's eleven entries in the 90 days before the occurrence were all faults present when written. The outgoing master believed the plotter had frozen three or four times on this vessel in the previous year, and it had frozen on the master a month earlier, with none of it written down.

Entries would have reached the Operations Manager's weekly review and the maintenance system, and from there the contractor, who needed one bench test to name the fix. However, the chain from an entry to an applied fix ran through someone ashore finding the manufacturer's bulletin, and the operator held no subscription to the bulletins, so a recorded freeze might have been reviewed, noted and left. [NOT ESTABLISHED: how many recorded freezes would have led to the unit being sent to the contractor, or how quickly, as the maintenance system holds nothing on the plotter in 2026]. On balance, it is likely that the defect procedure's failure to require a self-cleared fault to be recorded contributed to the plotter freeze in the channel.

The verbal handover at about 13:05 at the town wharf was an instance of that gap. The outgoing master told the master about both morning freezes, the master replied that it had done the same a month before, and neither made an entry. Both volunteered the omission, and both described the same rule. This omission was unlikely to have contributed in itself. An entry at 13:05 would have been reviewed at the end of the week, and nothing written that afternoon could have applied firmware to the unit, or removed the vessel from TF18, by 18:07. It increased risk because it was the practice rather than a lapse, and the fault passed by word of mouth left the next master knowing and everyone ashore not.

From the freeze to leaving the channel

The vessel was 1 m west of the centreline abeam the No. 2 beacon at 18:05:30 and held it within 3 m to the freeze. From 18:07:06 the heading increased from 195 to 200 degrees over about a minute and was then held. The rate of turn peaked at 6 degrees per minute at 18:07:40, while the master was at the frozen screen, and was back to zero by 18:08:50. Rudder angle followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees, so the turn was steered. There was no cross-set at that state of tide and the wind was offshore. The master said the vessel was eased to starboard while the master was at the plotter and then looking for the beacon, and that the master never made that decision. Nothing on the bridge showed the master the new heading, because the plotter symbol was frozen and the beacon was screened. Held at 200 degrees against the channel's 195, the heading moved the vessel west at about 20 m a minute, and it crossed the 20 m to the western edge at about 18:09:00. It is virtually certain that the heading change took the vessel out of the dredged channel.

The speed did not change. The track recorded 8.4 kt at the freeze and 8.1 kt at 18:08:00, and the fall to 7.1 kt by 18:11:48 was accounted for by shoaling drag, with no throttle movement until 18:11:52. The vessel crossed the western edge 114 seconds after the freeze. A crash stop begun before about 18:11:40 would have stopped it short of the contact point, and the vessel's trials figure for a crash stop from 8 kt is 92 m. There was no other traffic, the water was flat, and stopping cost nothing. The master said stopping was not considered because the master went straight to the visual transit, which in the master's mind was the backup. At 18:10:02 the master saw the beacon dead ahead and knew the vessel was off the line to the west. The master brought the vessel to port rather than stopping, because the master took the vessel to be just outside the edge, a boat width, when it was 39 m west of the centreline. The master said stopping on the edge of a bank that could not be seen felt worse than easing back. The course over ground came back from 200 to 197 degrees, still west of the channel's 195. No lookout was on the bridge after the deckhand was sent to collect fares at 18:04:14. This was normal practice on the route and OPS-3 did not address it either way. It is very likely that continuing at eight knots from the freeze until the shallow alarm contributed to the vessel leaving the channel and reaching the bank.

The heading change went unnoticed because the one reference that would have shown it was screened. The range and visibility check on 18/07/2026 found the No. 4 beacon not visible from the channel between 0.84 nm and 0.34 nm north of it, because the sightline passed through the canopy on Merrandi Islet. The canopy measured 5.8 m against a lantern height of 4.2 m. With the plotter frozen, the beacon was the only means of fixing left. The master began looking at 18:08:31, 0.47 nm north of it, and called it at 18:10:02 at 0.25 nm, 91 seconds later. Seen on the starboard bow where it belongs, the light would likely have shown the vessel drawing west within a minute of the turn, while it was still in the channel.

Two points count against this. The heading change began at 18:07:06, before the search started, so the screening explains why the turn went unnoticed and not why it began. The beacon was also clear of the islet for at least the last 37 seconds of the search, from about 18:09:25, and was not seen in that time. Neither point removes the effect of the screening over the minute and a half in which the vessel was still near the edge. The investigation concluded that it is likely that the screening of the beacon contributed to the heading change going unnoticed.

The screening itself followed from a deferral. Work order WO-118, raised in 09/2023, recorded the regrowth and recommended trimming to 2 m on a three-yearly cycle at an estimated $18,500. It was deferred at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 works rounds, each time as "defer, unfunded, refer next round". WO-176 in 03/2026 recorded the sightline as "now fully closed on the northern approach". The Authority's file note recorded that the islet is 240 m from the beacon and so outside the 50 m vegetation scope of schedule 2.4 of the services agreement, so the work competed with boat ramps and pontoons in the general waterways vote. The canopy grew from 2.1 m in 2019 to 5.8 m in 07/2026, about half a metre a year, so a trim funded at the 2023 round would have left it near 3.5 m on the night, under the 4.2 m lantern. The monthly check required by S2.1 was made from the town wharf, 2.1 nm south of the beacon, from which the islet is not in the line of sight, so it could not show the screening. The growth may not have been even over the seven years, since only two measurements exist. It is very likely that the deferral of the sightline clearing contributed to the beacon being screened.

The last defence was the echo sounder shallow alarm. It was set to 0.9 m under the keel, the value written at commissioning in 2019 and never changed. It sounded at 18:11:48, and both throttles went astern 4 seconds later, within the time that astern thrust was still developing. Contact followed at 18:12:04, 16 seconds after the alarm. At 7.1 kt the vessel covered 58 m in that time against a crash stop distance of 92 m. On the surveyed gradient of about 1 in 70, a setting of about 1.6 m under the keel would have sounded about 107 m short of the contact, enough for a crash stop with four seconds to react, and would still not have sounded in the dredged channel at low water. The alarm did what it was set to do. It is extremely likely that the 2019 setting, by giving 16 seconds' warning, contributed to the vessel reaching the bank at 6.8 kt.

Unresolved: unshielded floodlights behind the No. 4 beacon

The foreshore redevelopment commissioned on 22/05/2026, ten days before the winter timetable began, included 14 unshielded LED floodlights on 12 m columns at the new boat ramp, each presenting about 4,800 candela toward the channel. The survey of 18/07/2026 found that from 0.5 nm north of the beacon the array lies behind it within 4 degrees of the same bearing and within 1.5 degrees of the same elevation. The array is continuously lit while the beacon flashes green for 0.4 seconds every 2.5 seconds. The Port Authority's aids to navigation officer was not consulted and no assessment was made. The master described looking "into a wall of light" and the beacon as "a nothing" against the town and the car park. The outgoing master independently called it "washed out altogether from up the top". For at least the last 37 seconds before the master called the beacon it was clear of the islet and not seen, which is the stretch in which the floodlights rather than the canopy stood between the master and the light.

Several points count against this. Over most of the search the canopy screened the beacon, which would not have been visible against a black background either. The heading change began at the plotter before the search, so the floodlights cannot have caused the turn. No measurement was made on the night, only a survey eleven days later. Nothing establishes a detection threshold for a 0.4 second green flash against this background, and the master said twice that they could not tell whether the lights were why the beacon was not seen.

Whether the floodlights delayed the sighting in those last seconds could not be settled, and the evidence is evenly balanced. It would be settled by [NOT ESTABLISHED: a detection threshold, or an observation of the beacon against the array under the conditions of the night]. No conclusion is drawn from it and none is carried into the findings.

Unresolved: master fatigue

The case for fatigue rests on the following. The occurrence was on day nine of a twelve-day tour, on a split duty of 05:40 to 08:40 and 13:00 to 19:20, with a transit in the last hour and a quarter of a 13 hour 40 minute spread. The master recorded 6 hours 15 minutes of sleep the night before and said "I was tired. I'd be lying if I said otherwise." After seeing the beacon dead ahead the master eased back rather than stopping and misjudged the distance from the edge, as a boat width when it was nearly 40 m, which is the kind of misjudgement fatigue is expected to produce.

The case against rests on the same answer, in which the master said they were not fighting to stay awake and were not slow. The recorded performance agrees. Helm work held the centreline within 3 m for the first two minutes in the channel, the response to the shallow alarm took 4 seconds, the radio work after the grounding was complete and correct at the first attempt, and the decision not to refloat was made in about thirty seconds and was right. Six and a quarter hours of sleep is what the master said is normal on a split, and nothing else bears on the master's state.

Whether the master was fatigued during the transit stands as about as likely as not. No detailed fatigue assessment was made. Every decision that mattered on the night is either answered by another factor, namely the absence of a plan and hold point, or contradicted by the recorded data, so no finding follows from the matter. It remains unresolved and nothing from it is carried into the conclusions.

Other factors that increased risk

The notification, availability and recording duties of WAN-2 section 4.2 apply only to aids on a declared shipping channel, and the Merrandi Channel is not one. Section 4.3 requires only that the authority can demonstrate an inspection interval it has set itself, and neither it nor the services agreement requires any user to be told of a defect, a deferral or a change. These duties would not have reached this occurrence. A notice of a range change would not have made a light visible through a canopy, and an availability figure measures whether a light is lit, which this one was throughout. Section 4.1 applies to every aid, and the screening was left because the 50 m vegetation scope put the work in the general waterways vote and not because of the code. It is unlikely that the gap in the code contributed. The gap remains in what users of an undeclared channel are told, which the Authority can close by its own practice.

The solar conversion in 11/2025 halved the nominal range from 6 nm to 3 nm, and the investigator measured 2.6 nm. The chart correction lodged on 04/02/2026 was still pending on 07/07/2026, no local notice was issued, and the operator's passage plan still gave 6 M. It is unlikely that this contributed. A screened light is not made visible by being brighter, the master already knew the light was weaker, and the search from 0.47 nm to 0.25 nm ran well inside the measured range. The plan nevertheless described a light that was no longer there.

The winter roster put the darkness transit in the last hour and a quarter of a spread that ends 20 minutes inside the operator's 14 hour limit, on every day of a twelve-day tour. No relief master is rostered, and the fatigue diary the operator asks for is not collected. The roster could reach this occurrence only through fatigue, which was not established, and it is unlikely that it contributed. The exposure recurs on every darkness transit of the timetable.

The forward saloon lifejacket locker is a matter still being examined. The 2019 interior refit placed the kiosk counter in front of the locker under a minor modification notice that did not trigger a re-survey. The survey of 16/07/2026 found the locker face cannot be reached from 22 of the 34 forward saloon seats without passing behind the counter through a 0.6 m gap, and the muster placard directs passengers to a locker they cannot see from their seats. The operator says the same counter is fitted to its two other 24 m vessels. The locker did not affect the grounding, and it is unlikely that it influenced the outcome: the vessel was upright and stable, and all 38 passengers were in lifejackets by about 18:22. The deckhand, however, had to ask three passengers to move and pass the lifejackets over the counter. In a fire, a capsize risk or a night evacuation, passengers who cannot reach the locker without crew help would wait for it. It is very likely that this arrangement increased risk, while it remains under examination.

Considered and not found contributing

Tide set down below prediction and steering or propulsion failure were each tested and found very unlikely, for the reasons given under General. The floodlights, the fatigue question and the verbal handover are dealt with above, each at the strength the evidence supports.

Positive actions

The master stopped both engines 27 seconds after contact and did not restart them. The pan pan at 18:13:04 stated that the master was not attempting to refloat, 60 seconds after the vessel came to rest. The master addressed the passengers within 36 seconds of the impact, had the No. 2 starboard void sounded, reported 75 mm of ingress to Port Control at 18:17:05 and had it sounded every ten minutes. Survey later confirmed a 180 mm split in the starboard plating in way of that void, with ingress reaching about 260 mm by the time the vessel refloated at 00:20. Backing a holed vessel off the bank into deep water on a falling tide, with 38 passengers aboard and the damage unassessed, would have put a flooding compartment into the channel. The decision against it was made within a minute. It is very likely that stopping the engines and not attempting to refloat reduced risk.

These actions were sound, and they sit against a sequence in which the vessel left the channel without a position fix, without a plan that required it to stop, and with a beacon that could not be seen from the stretch in which the departure began. The investigation concluded that the absence of a night plan with a hold point, the unrecorded plotter faults, the screened beacon and the alarm setting together left no control that applied before the 16 seconds' warning from the shallow alarm.

Conclusions

These findings are made with respect to the occurrence and should not be read as apportioning blame or liability to any organisation or individual.

The standard of proof applied was "Likely or probable": a proposition is established at a probability of 65% or more and not established at 35% or less, and anything between is inconclusive.

Recommendations

This section records the safety action already taken and the recommendations made against the safety issues the investigation established.

Clearing of the beacon's sightline deferred unfunded for three works rounds

Work order WO-118 recorded the mangrove regrowth screening the No. 4 beacon, and the work was deferred unfunded at three works rounds because the islet lay 240 m from the beacon and outside the 50 m vegetation scope of schedule 2.4 of the services agreement. It is very likely that this deferral contributed to the screening of the beacon, because a trim funded at the 2023 round would have left the canopy near 3.5 m, below the 4.2 m lantern.

The Harbour Master, Kanooka Heads, funded work order WO-176 from the 2026 waterways contingency and had the Merrandi Islet canopy trimmed to 2 m on 24/07/2026. A three-yearly trimming cycle has been programmed, and the sightline is to be re-measured from the inbound track on completion. This action is closed. It addresses the screening at this beacon in full, but it does not change the scope of schedule 2.4, which would still place a screening canopy beyond 50 m of an aid in the general waterways vote.

Recommendation to the Port Authority and Kanooka Shire Council, as parties to the aids to navigation services agreement. The services agreement limited vegetation work to within 50 m of an aid, so work needed to keep an aid visible from the water it serves competed with other waterways items and was deferred. The Investigator in charge recommended that the agreement replace the 50 m vegetation scope at schedule 2.4 with a sightline test, so that such work is funded as an aid to navigation whatever its distance from the structure. The recommendation is open, with a response due 30/09/2026. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the response to this recommendation, due 30/09/2026]

No night passage plan or hold point for loss of the primary fix

The operator's passage plan for the Merrandi Channel was written for the daylight transit, named no hold point and gave no guidance on loss of the plotter. It is very likely that this absence contributed to the transit continuing at eight knots after the plotter froze, because the master had 114 seconds in which a stop would have left the vessel in the channel. The master and the outgoing master, interviewed separately, each said that stopping was the right answer and that no document asked for it.

No safety action has been recorded against this issue.

Recommendation to Tarrakin Ferries. The operator had no night passage plan for the Merrandi Channel and no rule on what to do if the primary means of position fixing was lost inside it. The Investigator in charge recommended that Tarrakin Ferries write a night passage plan for the channel before any further darkness transit, and that the plan name a hold point under which loss of the primary means of position fixing inside the channel requires the way to be taken off the vessel until the position is re-established by another means. The recommendation is open, with a response due 30/09/2026. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the response to this recommendation, due 30/09/2026]

Safety issues with no recorded action or recommendation

The investigation also established the following safety issues, and it holds no safety action and no recommendation against any of them.

  • The defect procedure in OPS-9 did not require a fault that had cleared itself to be recorded. It is likely that this contributed to the plotter freeze because freezes on the vessel's primary means of position fixing went unrecorded and the firmware fix was never applied.
  • The last service moved into darkness through change record CHG-2026-014 without reopening the daylight-only route risk assessment RRA-07. It is likely that this contributed to the absence of a night passage plan.
  • Section 4.2 of WAN-2 did not apply to the Merrandi Channel, so no notice or availability duty covered its beacons. This did not influence the occurrence and remains a risk.
  • The No. 4 beacon's nominal range was halved by the solar conversion without notice to channel users. This did not influence the occurrence and remains a risk.
  • The winter roster placed the darkness transit at the end of a split duty within 20 minutes of the spread limit, with no relief master. This did not influence the occurrence and remains a risk.
  • The forward saloon lifejacket locker was blocked by a counter fitted in 2019 without re-survey, and the operator says the same counter is fitted to its two other 24 m vessels. This matter is still being examined.

For the solar conversion, local notice to waterway users LNM-2026-14 was issued on 22/07/2026, giving the conversion and the 3 M nominal range. The Port Authority's aids to navigation register was made available to every commercial operator using the channel, and Tarrakin Ferries reissued the passage plan appendix as issue 3 with the corrected range. This action by the Aids to Navigation Officer, Kanooka Shire Council, is in progress. It addresses the range change in part, because it corrects the information for this beacon but does not create a duty to notify users of future changes.

reviewNotes:
- [Factual information] - Critical event and notification TFP-OCC-2026-0093 record the vessel heeled 4 degrees to starboard. The master's 18:13:04 pan pan describes it as "upright". The draft reports both. - Factor "Unshielded boat ramp floodlights aligned behind the No. 4 beacon from the north": no factual description of the lights (position, shielding, alignment, date) appears in the evidence. The masters refer to "car park" lighting, not boat ramp lighting. - Factor "Darkness transit rostered to close a split duty within 20 minutes of the spread limit": the spread limit itself is not recorded anywhere. - Factor "Last service moved into darkness without reopening the daylight-only risk assessment": no extract of the risk assessment is held. The only source is the master's account of the passage plan. - Merrandi Islet canopy height: 5.8 m measured on 18/07/2026 against 2.1 m in the 2019 aerial survey. - The lifejacket and lookout facts rest partly on the deckhand interview, which is not finalised. - [Analysis / External Influences] - Aids code factor, Importance text: it states that the solar conversion "reached nobody for eight months". The Port Authority records show that a notification was lodged with the hydrographic service on 04/02/2026. The claim holds for channel users and operators only, and the draft words it that way. The investigator may wish to tighten the Importance text to match. - Aids code factor, Importance text: the "96-passenger ferry" figure appears only in the investigator's Importance argument. No factual source for the vessel's passenger capacity is given in the material supplied for this pass. - Port Authority records, WO-118: the 09/2023 work order places the screening between approximately half a mile and a quarter mile. The 18/07/2026 check measured it at 0.84 nm to 0.34 nm. This is probably explained by canopy growth (2.1 m in 2019, 5.8 m in 2026) and by WO-176 recording the sightline as fully closed. The two extents should still not be presented as the same measurement. - [Analysis / Organisational Influences] - Darkness transit rostered to close a split duty: the investigator note says the factor was "split out of the old roster object on 09/10/2026", which is after the generation date of 2026-10-08. - Clearing of the beacon's sightline: WO-118 describes the screening as between about half a mile and a quarter mile, while the 18/07/2026 check measured 0.84 nm to 0.34 nm. These may reflect growth between 2023 and 2026, but no measurement in between is held to confirm this. - Beacon's range halved by solar conversion: the master's words are quoted in the factor's evidence fields, but no verbatim interview extract is attached, so the draft summarises them rather than quoting them. - [Analysis / Risk Controls] - No night passage plan or hold point, Influence note: a crash stop "begun before about 18:11:40" is said to stop short of contact. At the recorded 7.1 to 7.6 kt, 18:11:40 is about 24 seconds or roughly 88 m from contact, against a trials crash-stop figure of 92 m from 8 kt. The margin depends on the lower speed and is not shown. The basis for the 18:11:40 figure may need stating. - Forward saloon lifejacket locker: the factor's evidence says the deckhand asked three passengers to move away from the counter. The deckhand's recorded words at 18:22:40 refer to two passengers he had to go round the servery for. These may describe different things, but the two counts should be reconciled or distinguished. - [Analysis / Local Conditions] - Master fatigued during the channel transit: the investigator note says the factor was split out "on 09/10/2026", which is after the date the material was generated (08/10/2026). - Master fatigued during the channel transit: the evidence says the centreline was held to within 3 m "for the first two minutes in the channel". The AIS track shows it was held from 18:03:58 to 18:07:06, which is over three minutes. - No. 4 beacon screened by mangroves, and Unshielded boat ramp floodlights: both carry an arrow to "Heading eased five degrees to starboard without a decision to turn". Yet each factor's own evidence states that it cannot have caused the turn, which began at 18:07:06, before the search at 18:08:31. The edge appears to go to the holding of the heading and its going unnoticed, not to its onset. The event title may need to reflect that. - Unshielded boat ramp floodlights: the factor carries a "Led to" arrow despite an inconclusive influence test. - [Analysis / Individual Actions] - Engines stopped and no attempt made to refloat: the evidence says the pan pan was made "60 seconds after the vessel came to rest". The 60 seconds runs from contact at 18:12:04 to 18:13:04. The audio records about 9 seconds of grinding after contact, so the vessel came to rest at about 18:12:13, roughly 51 seconds before the pan pan. The draft does not state the 60-second figure. - Plotter fault passed on verbally: the Influence test note refers to "a year of freezes that were never written down". The evidence given for this factor shows only the two freezes that morning and the relieving master's mention of a freeze "the month before". The year-long history is not supported in the material given here and may sit on the procedure object. - [Analysis / Occurrence Events] - Shallow alarm at its 2019 setting of 0.9 m gave sixteen seconds' warning, Influence note: the sentence "A setting that gave forty seconds would" does not give the under-keel value of that setting, so the report cannot state what setting would have sounded in the dredged channel at low water. The investigator may wish to supply the figure. - Vessel left the dredged channel on the bank side, Evidence: the text describes the heading increasing from 195 to 200 degrees, but the AIS table gives course over ground for those values. The rate of turn supports a heading change, but the two quantities are used interchangeably and may need reconciling. - [Conclusions] - Heading eased five degrees / Vessel left the dredged channel: the collation gives the heading change as 195 to 200 degrees. The approved Factual information says it reached 199 degrees at 18:08:31 and was held there. - Vessel left the dredged channel: the collation places the vessel 1 m west of the charted centreline abeam No. 2 at 18:05:30. The approved Factual information says it was on the centreline. - Transit continued at eight knots: the collation gives 7.1 kt by 18:11:48. The approved Recorded data gives 7.6 kt by 18:11. These may be consistent, but the two figures should be reconciled. - Darkness transit rostered: the collation gives the operator's limits (10 hours of duty, 14 hours of spread). The approved Personnel information still carries a NOT ESTABLISHED marker for the spread limit and the margin to it. - Unshielded boat ramp floodlights: the collation gives the position, output and commissioning date (22/05/2026). The approved Channel and site information still carries a NOT ESTABLISHED marker for these. - Unshielded boat ramp floodlights and No. 4 beacon screened: both causal chains run to the heading change. The recorded heading change began at 18:07:06, before the search for the beacon began at 18:08:31, so the edge to the turn itself runs backwards in time. Only the turn's going unnoticed can follow from these conditions. - Darkness transit rostered, Master fatigued, Heading eased: the investigator notes are dated 09/10/2026, which is after the collation's generation date of 2026-10-08. - Forward saloon lifejacket locker: the object is not finalised, pending the operator's and regulator's answers on the fleet-wide question, but it appears as a finding here. - [Recommendations / Clearing of the beacon's sightline deferred unfunded for three works rounds] - Recommendation on schedule 2.4 scope: the record names the investigator in charge as the raiser but does not name the addressee organisation. It also does not identify the parties to the aids to navigation services agreement. The addressee needs to be confirmed. - Recommendation on schedule 2.4 scope: the response was due 30/09/2026 and the item is still shown as Open. That date has passed as of the generation date of 08/10/2026. The response status should be confirmed before publication. - [Recommendations / Last service moved into darkness without reopening the daylight-only risk assessment] - Safety issue "Last service moved into darkness without reopening the daylight-only risk assessment": Importance is recorded as Not tested. The section asks for the issue's safety significance, so the significance above rests on the Influence argument alone. - Investigation log, 2026-07-08 entry: the General Manager Operations suspended evening Muntari services. This is not recorded as a safety action against this issue, and the record does not say whether TF18 is among those services. It has not been included. The investigator may wish to confirm whether it should be recorded as action taken against this issue. - Approved Analysis text, "Last service moved into darkness...": the statement "The daylight restriction is not referenced anywhere in the change" does not appear in the evidence for this factor as given. Only the investigator note ("approved by somebody else who never saw it") points that way. The supporting extract should be checked against it. - Evidence against influence on the same factor: the Operations Manager's account "has not been taken as a formal interview". This is an open line of enquiry. The report text states only that his understanding was not established. - [Recommendations / No night passage plan or hold point for loss of the primary fix] - Recommendation to Tarrakin Ferries: the recorded response date of 30/09/2026 has passed. The issue still shows as Open and no response is recorded. - Investigation log entry 2026-07-08: the General Manager Operations suspended the evening Muntari services after the occurrence. This is not recorded as a safety action against this issue. If it is one, it would address the issue in part, because it removes darkness transits but provides no plan or hold point. The investigator should confirm whether it belongs here. - Significance for "No night passage plan or hold point" says "every master asked said they would have used one". The investigator notes and the recommendation refer to two masters interviewed. The draft uses the narrower wording. - [Recommendations / Defect procedure never requires a fault that cleared itself to be recorded] - Defect procedure safety issue: the section brief asks for the issue's Importance, but Importance is marked "Not tested" on this object. The significance above is therefore carried on the Influence result alone. - Plotter fault passed on verbally at the change of master: this instance failed Influence (unlikely), while the procedure it exemplifies passed Influence (likely) through the same non-recording mechanism. The two results may be consistent, since a single entry at 13:05 could not have produced a fix by 18:07. The record does not state that reasoning, so the investigator may wish to make it explicit. - [Recommendations / Beacon's range halved by solar conversion with no notice to channel users] - Safety action (LNM-2026-14, register release, passage plan issue 3): status is recorded as "In progress", but every component is described as already done. The record does not say which part remains open. - Approved Analysis text states "The aids to navigation register has never been provided to the operator", but the safety action states the register has been made available to every commercial operator. This reads as a tense or timing conflict that the investigator may wish to reconcile. - The approved Analysis text that discusses section 4.2 of the aids code appears immediately above a heading for this issue. That text appears to belong to the factor "Aids code set no notice or availability duty for beacons off declared channels", so the placement of the heading may need checking. - Importance note: the issue is recorded as "answered in part", but the record does not say what part remains unanswered. The chart correction, still pending on 07/07/2026, is not covered by the recorded safety action. - [Recommendations / Darkness transit rostered to close a split duty within 20 minutes of the spread limit] - Darkness transit roster factor, investigator notes: the factor is recorded as "Split out of the old roster object on 09/10/2026". That date is one day after the stated generation date of 2026-10-08. - Darkness transit roster factor, Importance text versus the approved Analysis: the Importance text says the operator asks for a fatigue diary and "never reads" it. The approved Analysis says the operator "does not collect it". These describe different failures. The investigator may wish to confirm which is correct. The draft above uses neutral wording ("is not acted on") pending that. - [Recommendations / Forward saloon lifejacket locker blocked by a 2019 counter fitted without re-survey] - Forward saloon lifejacket locker, Importance test note and Investigator notes: these say whether the defect is fleet-wide still waits on the operator's and the regulator's answers. The Evidence line and the Importance paragraph say the operator has already answered, on 16/07, that the same counter is fitted to its two other 24 m vessels. It is unclear whether the operator's answer is in, whether only the regulator's answer is pending, or whether the operator's statement still awaits confirmation. - Forward saloon lifejacket locker, Note on Influence: "ashore within 74" gives no unit. Minutes is the apparent meaning, but the record does not say so. - Forward saloon lifejacket locker, Significance: the figure of forty lifejackets appears only in the Significance text and is not given in the Evidence line or the survey summary. It has been left out of the draft until it is confirmed against the stowage survey extract. - [Executive summary] - Heading eased five degrees to starboard: the approved Factual information gives the heading as reaching 199 degrees at 18:08:31 and held there. The heading-change and vessel-departure factors, and approved finding 13, give 195 to 200 degrees. This summary follows 200. - Engines stopped and no attempt made to refloat: the positive event places the decision "within a minute" (pan pan 60 seconds after contact). The fatigue and roster factors say "about thirty seconds". Approved finding 14 says within a minute, and the Other findings bullet on fatigue says about thirty seconds. - Darkness transit rostered and Heading eased factors: investigator notes are dated 09/10/2026, which is after the generation date of 2026-10-08. - Approved Factual information, Personnel information, carries [NOT ESTABLISHED] for the spread limit. The roster factor gives the limit as 14 hours with a 20 minute margin, and approved finding 5 states it. Similarly, the floodlight position and commissioning date (22/05/2026) and the RRA-07 date and content are marked [NOT ESTABLISHED] in Factual information but are given in the factors. - Safety actions: both recommendations show a response due 30/09/2026 and are still recorded as Open.
